title: As a self-hoster, I can install the assistant on my own machine with one documented command — installer script, npm/pip package, or Docker image — and reach a working chat in minutes
As a self-hoster, official deployment paths cover my target — Docker Compose, Kubernetes/Helm, a small VPS, or a Raspberry Pi — each with its own maintained guide
As an everyday user, a first-run wizard walks me through model credentials, channels, and defaults instead of hand-editing config files
As a self-hoster, updating is safe and documented — versioned releases with changelogs, migration notes, and a repair or rollback path when an update breaks
As an everyday user, I can talk to my assistant from the messengers I already use — WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord, Slack, or iMessage — not just a bespoke web page
As a self-hoster, inbound messages are gated — sender allowlists, DM policies, mention gating — so only people I approve can drive my assistant
As a power user, I can interact by voice — voice notes get transcribed, replies can be spoken, or live voice conversations are supported
As an everyday user, the assistant also meets me in official web, desktop, or mobile apps with feature parity beyond the chat basics
As a power user, I can plug in multiple model providers — Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, OpenRouter, and more — and switch models per agent or per conversation
As a privacy-first user, I can run the assistant entirely on local models — Ollama, llama.cpp, LM Studio, or vLLM — with no cloud model dependency
As a self-hoster, I bring my own API keys or subscriptions and can see token usage and cost per model or per conversation
As a self-hoster, model failover keeps the assistant working — automatic fallback to another provider or model when one errors or rate-limits
As a power user, I can browse a real skills/plugins registry and install a capability with one command or click
As a developer, I can write my own skill, tool, or plugin against a documented format and load it into my instance locally
As a power user, the community ecosystem is genuinely alive — thousands of published skills, plugins, or presets with active maintainers
As a security engineer, the skills/plugin registry has a security story — scanning or moderation, provenance, and a documented response to malicious submissions
As an everyday user, the assistant remembers me across sessions — durable long-term memory it can write to and recall from automatically
As a power user, I can attach my own documents and notes as a knowledge base and get grounded answers over them
As a privacy-first user, I can inspect, edit, and delete what the assistant has remembered — the memory store lives on my machine in an open format
As a power user, the assistant can run commands and edit files on my machine — a real exec surface, not just chat about what to do
As a power user, the assistant can drive a real browser — navigate, log in, click, and extract from live pages on my behalf
As a power user, the assistant reaches beyond one machine — paired phones and computers it can use for screenshots, camera, notifications, or media playback
As a developer, the assistant can supervise or embed real coding agents so it does repo work — cloning, editing, testing — not just snippets in chat
As a security engineer, credentials are handled deliberately — a secrets store or env separation with redaction, never API keys pasted into chat history
As a security engineer, risky tool runs are containable — container/VM sandboxing, tool policies, or permission modes that limit what the agent can touch
As a self-hoster, dangerous actions require my explicit approval — command allowlists, approval prompts, and elevated modes that are opt-in per action
As a power user, I can run multiple distinct agents with their own prompts, models, and workspaces, and route conversations or channels to each
As an AI-native user, agents can work together — subagents, swarms, or an agent-to-agent protocol that splits and parallelizes real work
